title: The Future of Fabrics and Fibres

paragraphs.text: Early synthetic materials from the mid-twentieth century often clung to the wearer due to static electricity, which also made the fabric collect dirt. These chemically produced textiles were often uncomfortable as they did not allow the wearer's body to breathe. In comparison, highly sophisticated modern synthetics have none of these disadvantages and can create efficient barriers to rain, wind and snow while being totally breathable. Today's synthetics can be renamed to distinguish them from former inventions—for example, polyamide is often the preferred name for nylon.

Modern synthetic threads are produced by the extrusion of the chemical, forcing it through fine holes. The materials produced are incredibly versatile and capable of being moulded into many different forms during the liquid stage of their manufacture. This flexibility means that fibres can be made to exact specification. Some are ultra-lightweight and high-stretch, others are thin and light-reflective, while hollow fibres trap air to retain heat and keep the body warm. A wide range of visual effects can be achieved. However, even when superfine, transparent and fragile-looking, these new synthetics are still very strong, durable and easy to care for.

Synthetic fibres' recent gain in appeal is partly due to the invention of microfibres. Most are derived from coal-and-oil-based raw material and offer easy-care and quick-drying fabrics. Combinations of microfibres with regenerated yarns, cottons, linens, silks and other synthetics are often successful in creating new looks, better handling and added performance. For example, a microfibre combined with cotton (chosen for its appearance and absorbency) gives the resulting textile a natural appeal with built-in technical properties. Microfibres can be altered at any stage of their manufacture—from the fibre to the finishing of the fabric, and this is what makes them the real future of textiles.

A microfibre is by definition one in which the yarn is 1/60th of the thickness of an average human hair, or less. Ultra-microfibres are now on the market which are infinitely fine—up to 1/200th of the same thickness. Because they are super-fine, specific qualities and functions can be built in. With the thinnest fibres, these are greater possibilities to create fabrics with a soft, sheer appearance. They can be delicate, attractive to handle, ultra-light in weight, crease-resistant, and possess excellent draping qualities. Microfibre fabrics are machine-washable and will not lose their shape. The fibres are so fine that it is possible to construct fabrics dense enough to be windproof and breathable, which means they can prevent the smallest drop of water from entering while allowing perspiration to pass through as water vapour. These fabrics can maintain an even body temperature in both hot and cold conditions, keeping the wearer comfortable.

Using the latest in microtechnology, scientists are building fabrics where the fibre itself is scrutinized in minute detail. Microfibres have been developed by textile professionals who made close studies of microfibres in the nature and took advantage of technological breakthroughs, which allow the manipulation of molecules.

When looking at a micro-world to create advanced materials, the potential is almost limitless, and the resulting microfibres are now being developed to create new synthetic fabrics with distinctive aesthetic, tactile and performance properties.

Research and development into high performance textiles for extreme sportswear is where much investment has taken place. Clothing and accessories for the fast-growing area of sport, in all its guises, has meant the invention of a range of materials with incredible properties. As a result, sportswear and other high-performance clothing is where the majority of microfibre applications can be seen. However, the creative potential in working with fabrics constructed with microfibres is extensive.

Microtechnology and health is another strong area of research and development. New textiles that can look attractive, feel good and perform well can now even benefit the wearer's health. Microfibres are being engineered with substances suspended in bubbles that can be gradually released. These bubbles are hollow and can contain a range of products, including medication, natural remedies, antibacterial /anti-microbial agents and insect repellents. These ingredients are invisible to the eye and yet can have a dramatic effect.

Many of these microfibres were originally developed for use in space but are now being used in fashion and for the lingerie and hosiery markets. The Japanese are even developing youth-giving textiles which encapsulate anti-ageing creams into fabrics worn next to the skin. This microencapsulation technique works when the seals around the tiny capsules are broken by the fabric being creased or rubbed. The contents are absorbed slowly through the skin. Even the warmth of the body makes, for example, a fragrance incorporated into the material become stronger.
